case_name: Christian Jew Foundation v. Christian Jew Outreach
text:
Christian Jew Foundation
and Hedrick v. Christian Jew Outreach et al.

Court File No.
03-CV0-249068CM1

R. Cosman and D. Gourley,
counsel for the plaintiffs

T. Corbett, counsel for the
defendants

Heard:  January 11, 30 and
31 and February 1, 2006

Endorsement

In this action, Master Kelly heard part of the plaintiffs’
motion to compel answers to undertakings and refusals.  Master Kelly was not
able to complete the hearing of the motion due to his retirement.  Upon his
retirement, Master Kelly released reasons dated May 20, 2005 (the “Kelly
decision”) with respect to certain of the undertakings and refusals.  I heard
the balance of the plaintiffs’ motion to compel answers to undertakings and
refusals (the “refusals motion”).

In addition, the plaintiffs’ brought a motion for a
further and better affidavit of documents (the “production motion”).
Initially, the production motion was scheduled for hearing on January 11, 2006
and submissions were commenced on that date.  However, it became clear over the
course of submissions that there was some overlap of issues as between the
production motion and the refusals motion.  Accordingly, the production motion
was adjourned to January 30 and 31, 2006, dates that had been previously set
aside for the hearing of the refusals motions.

The Production Motion

On
the production motion, counsel for the plaintiffs submitted that the plaintiffs
are entitled to a further and better affidavit of documents from the defendants
for the following reasons:

1
.

1.

the
defendants disclosed and produced their documents on a piece meal basis over
time (upon the original affidavit of documents, at discoveries, by answers to
undertakings, upon the return of the refusals motion before Master Kelly, by
attachments to affidavits filed in response to motions and pursuant to the
Kelly endorsement);

2
.

2.

as
a result of the disclosure production over time, the affidavit of documents and
the supplementary affidavit of documents do not allow for cross-referencing and
the documents have been produced in a fashion that does not allow the
plaintiffs to have any confidence that they have received all of the documents
disclosed (page numbers, etc. are confusing);

3
.

3.

the
defendants have not produced further documents that must now be disclosed on
account of the amendment of the statement of claim (the amendment related to
the plaintiffs’ request for an accounting and repayment of donations); and

4
.

4.

there
are documents that the plaintiffs’ accountant deposes that have not been produced
and which documents are required to provide a full accounting of the funds
advanced by Christian Jew Foundation (“CJF”) to Christian Jew Outreach (“CJO”).

Some
background is necessary to understand the context within which the production
motion arises.  Upon the plaintiffs’ retainer of new counsel, new counsel
advised the defendants’ counsel that he could not locate the defendants’
supplemental affidavit of documents.  In response, the defendants’ counsel
advised plaintiffs’ counsel that he had provided a copy to former counsel of
record and, further, defence counsel provided an additional supplemental
affidavit of documents, albeit in draft form.  Plaintiffs’ counsel had some
difficulty with the draft supplemental affidavit of documents because it was
not sworn and there was reference to page numbers, the relevance of which was
unknown.

In
addition, further documents had been provided as a result of answers to
undertakings and the questions ordered answered by Master Kelly.  However,
plaintiffs’ counsel has not been able to cross-reference these documents to the
draft supplemental affidavit of documents.

As
well, prior to the pending motion, defence counsel advised that he would update
and deliver a further supplemental affidavit of documents but, as of the
hearing, it had not been provided as defence counsel wished to await the
disposition of the court on the production issue.  Defence counsel did not
object to the delivery of a sworn supplemental affidavit of documents, but did
object to the scope of production that the plaintiffs now seek.

Thus,
the major issue on this motion was whether the defendants ought to produce the
documents identified by the plaintiffs in Schedule “A” to the plaintiffs’ factum,
this schedule being a list of documents compiled by the plaintiffs’ expert, Mr.
Gottschalk, as supported in his affidavit (the “Gottschalk affidavit”).

The
issue, according to the plaintiffs, is the sufficiency of production.  For
example, the plaintiffs refer to the Gottschalk affidavit to support their
allegation that there are broad categories of financial and accounting records
or documents that are relevant and necessary and that exist, according to CJO
(see for eg. p. 67 of the motion record for a list of the records CJO claims it
keeps).

In
addition to the Gottschalk affidavit, the plaintiffs rely upon the Kelly
decision, wherein Master Kelly ordered production of a specified list of
financial records, for the following reasons:

“These questions shall be answered and the documents
referred to in (a) to (h) above, if within the possession or control of CJO,
shall be produced.  This action addresses the proper accounting between the
parties and the integrity of the parties in their dealings with one another.
The nature and quality of CJO’s record keeping and compliance with statutory
requirements, has semblance of relevance to the pleaded issues, and the
documents referred to above directly impact that issue.”

Lastly,
it is submitted that CJO engaged an accountant, Mr. LeGrow, to keep its books
and records and, thus, the books and records must exist.

The
crux of CJO’s response to the production motion is that it has produced enough
documents and that the plaintiffs’ request for further production amounts to an
abuse of process.  In this regard, CJO’s counsel takes the position that so
long as it can establish that it has properly applied an amount of funds
equivalent to the amount of CJF’s advances to “charitable works”, that is
sufficient to answer the claims in the action.  As I understand the submission,
CJO takes the view that, if CJF advanced $1 million, CJO need only establish
the expenditure of $1 million on charitable works, regardless of other receipts
of donations and expenditures.  CJO takes the position on the production motion
that it is not necessary to examine what other amounts it received from non-CJF
sources or that it expended any amount beyond the amount of advances it
received from CJF.

I
do not accept CJO’s position.  In my view, the pleadings set forth the allegation
that CJO was formed as the Canadian branch of the CJF and to the extent that
CJO raised funds, in addition to the funds obtained directly from CJF, the
proper use of all of the funds generally and of the CJF funds in particular are
relevant.  I agree with the dicta of Master Kelly that the entirety of the
relationship between CJF and CJO, and as between the other parties, is the
central issue in the action.

There
was some dispute as to what Master Kelly ordered by way of production.  In my
view, it is clear that Master Kelly ordered production of the specified
documents “as required by CCA” and the ruling was circumscribed.  On this
motion, the plaintiffs seek a wider scope of documents, as delineated by Mr. Gottschalk.
Master Kelly’s ruling does not address these additional categories of
documents.  All financial and accounting records, not merely those required to
be maintained by the CCA, must be produced as they have a semblance of
relevance.  Plaintiffs’ counsel reassured the court that not every scrap of
paper was required and that there would be a narrowing of the scope of
documents required.  In my view, while I rule that the financial and accounting
records must be produced, I would require the defendants to produce financial
and accounting records, books and ledger and thereafter, require the plaintiffs
to specify and identify with some precision as to the particular document they
require.  I have in mind that some items in the accounting may not be issues
(for eg. utility payments) and thus, I do not expect that the defendants to be
obliged to produce such documents.

In
my view, it may well be that CJO can establish a minimum level of proper
expenditure.  This very evidence might be available to satisfy other donors.
In my view, given the breadth of the allegations against CJO and Israel, and
Israel’s counterclaim of defamation, the use of all receipts is relevant or has
a semblance of relevance to the issues in the action.

In
addition, in my view, it is not appropriate, at this stage of the action, to
render a ruling on whether evidence of expenditures for charitable works in an
amount equal to the amount of CJF advances is sufficient to account for the CJF
funds or whether some broader requirement is necessary.  That is the role and
function of the trial judge, who will have to determine whether CJO breached
its obligations to CJF.

In
addition, CJO objects to further production on the basis that it has had a law
clerk review all supporting documents and complete an analysis of CJO’s use of
funds.  In my view, the fact that CJO may be able to demonstrate where the
funds were spent, conclusively from their perspective, does not mitigate their
disclosure obligations and I accept the submission of plaintiffs’ counsel that
the plaintiffs are not obliged to simply accept the defendants’ word, or that
of a law clerk employed by defence counsel, that the CJF advances have been
properly expended.

Lastly,
CJO objects to the Gottschalk affidavit on the basis that Gottschalk is an
“advocate”.  I have reviewed the Gottschalk affidavit and the transcript and I
do not agree that Mr. Gottschalk acted as an “advocate”.  Clearly, he formed
his views and opinions on the scope of the records required, having regard to
what had been produced.

In
any event, in determining the weight to be given to the Gottschalk affidavit I
must consider the evidence put forth in response to the motion.  On this
motion, CJO has adduced the affidavit of Israeli who admittedly has no
financial or accounting experience.  He relied upon CJO’s bookkeeper of 5
years, Mr. LeGrow and/or its auditor, Mr. Ahyre.  CJO did not file any
affidavit material from these witnesses.  In my view, I am entitled to draw an
adverse inference from this failure.  I find no merit to CJO’s submissions as
to the questionable weight to be given to the Gottschalk affidavit.

I
note as well that CJO does not take the position that the documents are not
relevant.  Its primary objection is that the significant amount of work
necessary to obtain production is not warranted having regard to the fact that
CJO has produced proof of expenditures to the amount of the CJF advances.

It
is my conclusion that CJO must deliver a properly sworn further and better
affidavit of documents.  The further and better affidavit of documents shall be
delivered within 60 days of the date hereof and shall include the documents
listed in Schedule “A” to the plaintiffs’ factum.  Further, the further and
better affidavit of document shall comprise a complete list of all documents
produced, identified by sequential numbers and cross referenced by the date of
production, the source (eg. discoveries or answers to undertakings) and the
number of pages in the document.   In addition, the defendants shall produce
for inspection their own copies of the productions, in the same order as the
further and better affidavit of documents, so as to permit the plaintiffs to
satisfy themselves as to the completeness of the productions.

For
the time being, I would not require all of the back up or source documents in
5.2, 7.2, 7.3.3, 8.2 (I would require the statements for the Russian VISA/Mastercard),
10 and 11.4 (to be produced only as to the specified matters).  The plaintiffs
shall review the statements upon production and identify the source documents
required thereafter.

If
there are any difficulties in the production process, I may be spoken to.

The
court raised the issue of the timing of the motion – i.e. whether the documents
sought ought to have been requested on discovery or a motion brought prior to
the commencement of discoveries.  I accept the submissions of counsel for the
plaintiffs that the defendants have an ongoing obligation to produce relevant
documents, that discoveries have not yet been completed, in view of the re-attendance
required for the purpose of dealing with the undertakings and refusals and
follow up questions and the amendment of the statement of claim.  The
plaintiffs rely upon the decisions in Bow Helicopters v. Textdrawn Canada Ltd.

[1981] OJ 2265 (Master)
at paras. 18-19
and Comtax Commodity Tax Consultants v.
Umbrella Communications Inc.
[2002] OJ 4537 (Master)
at para. 9
.  I have
reviewed these decisions and I do not read them as supporting the propositions
put forward by plaintiffs’ counsel.  However, I am persuaded that the ongoing
obligation to produce, particularly in light of the amendment to the statement
of claim herein, is ample authority to permit the bringing of the motion at
this stage of the litigation.

The Refusals Motion

In dealing with this aspect of the motion and in my
rulings as to whether or not a question must be answered, both parties accept
that the court must apply the test of relevance or semblance or relevance.

Schedule A

Question 1426:  On consent, the defendants shall confirm
that the stated full time salary of $3,166.66 is on a monthly basis.

Question 1428:  This question is relevant as to the
expenditures of funds by CJO and the accounting relief requested by the
plaintiffs.  The question is to be answered.

Question 1461:  On consent, the defendants shall confirm
that all board resolutions were contained in the minute book and have been
produced.

Question 1609-11:  The defendants indicated that they have
made inquiries and, thus, the answer is pending.  The defendants shall advise
the plaintiffs of any response and, if no response is forthcoming from Big
Star, the defendants shall advise as to the nature of their efforts to comply
and produce copies of request letters, if any.

Question 1684:  This question is relevant to the use of CJF funds, a central
issue in the action.  The plaintiffs are entitled to have the documents
regarding the receipt of funds, where the funds were deposited and how the
funds were spent.  This question must be answered.

Question 1780:  This question seeking electronic document
of Mr. LeGrow, CJO’s bookkeeper, is relevant.  The defendants must investigate
whether electronic documents of Mr. LeGrow exist and, if so, produce all
relevant documents.

Question 2018:  The defendants have agreed to answer this
question.  The question as to the date of creation of Exhibit 12 (which shows
how the advances from CJF to CJO were “booked”) is relevant.

Question 2022:  On consent, this question is to be
answered.

Question 2101:  On consent, the defendants shall confirm
the identities of the missionaries.

Question 2126-2157:  This question has been answered and
the defendants shall confirm the names provided.

Question 2494:  On consent, this question is to be
answered.

Question 2906:  On consent, the 2003 income tax return
will be produced.

Question 2996:  On consent, this question, relating to Mr.
LeGrow, is to be answered.

Question 3263:  The defendants have made inquiries of Big
Star and the response is pending.  Copies of the correspondent between the
defendants and Big Star regarding the documents are to be produced.

Question 3271:  The defendants have made inquiries of Big
Star and the response is pending.  The defendants shall produce the licence
agreement.

Question 3276:  The defendants have made inquires of Big
Star and the response is pending.

Question 3312:  This question is to be answered.  The
plaintiffs are prepared to await the response pending the defendants’ receipt
of response from Big Star.

Schedule B

Question 1136:  These documents are relevant to the use of
the funds advance by CJF to CJO.  The question must be answered.

Questions 1188, 1197, 1202:   The expenditure of CJF
advances, and whether and to what extent the expenditures were made in the
Soviet Union, is relevant.  These questions must be answered.

Question 1473, 1551, 1681:  The supporting documentation
must be produced.  The plaintiff is entitled to test the veracity of the
statements relied upon by the defendants.

Question 1904:  This question must be answered.  The
defendants rely upon expenditures in the Soviet Union in support of their claim
that CJF funds were put towards “charitable works”.  These questions are
relevant to the expenditures and must be answered.

Orders
to go

in
accordance with the above;

the
defendants shall re-attend to answer all proper follow up questions
arising from the questions ordered pursuant to the Kelly endorsement and
as ordered herein, unless the parties agree otherwise.  If a date cannot
be agreed upon by the parties, I may be spoken to;

Master
Kelly ordered the defendants to re-attend at the plaintiffs expense with
respect to the aspects of the motion disposed of by him.  With respect to
the matters disposed of herein, I order the re-attendance at the
defendants’ expense.  If necessary, the parties may speak to me on the
issue of apportionment upon the completion of the re-attendance and the
availability of the transcript; and

costs
of the motion are reserved and, if the parties cannot agree on the issues
of costs, written submissions may be delivered as follows:
